'''Joella Hardeman Gipson-Simpson''' (January 8, 1929 – January 31, 2012) was an American musician, mathematician, and educator who became the first [[African Americans|African American]] student at [[Mount St. Mary's University (Los Angeles)|Mount St. Mary's College]] in [[Los Angeles]].{{r|obit|remembering}}

==Early life and music education==
Joella Hardeman was born in Los Angeles on January 8, 1929, and began studying music at age eight. After graduating from Saint Agnes High School,{{r|obit}} a Catholic school in Los Angeles that operated from 1919 to 1953,{{r|agnes}} she entered [[Mount St. Mary's College]], becoming the first African American student accepted there.{{r|obit}} She majored in music performance and minored in English and philosophy, graduating in 1950,{{r|obit|remembering}} and won a graduate scholarship to the [[State University of Iowa]], where she earned a master's degree in [[music education]] in 1951.{{r|obit}}

With this, she began a career in music education, teaching at a number of institutions, including [[Southern University]] in [[Baton Rouge, Louisiana]],{{r|obit}} where she was listed in 1955 as a faculty sponsor for the local chapter of the [[Music Educators National Conference]].{{r|menc}} At Southern University, she met Theodore Horace Gipson, who became her husband and the father of her daughter.

==Later life and mathematics education==
Joella Gipson and her husband moved back to Los Angeles,{{r|obit}} and Joella Gipson became a teacher and supervisor for the [[Los Angeles Unified School District]].{{r|obit|msmcm}} It was in this part of her life that her interests shifted to mathematics, and she became certified as a mathematics teacher,{{r|obit}} regularly attending [[National Science Foundation]] sponsored mathematics institutes from 1958 to 1969.{{r|msmcm}} Her husband Theodore Gipson died in Los Angeles in 1972.{{r|obit}}

In 1971, Gipson earned a doctorate in mathematics education from the [[University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign]],{{r|msmcm|diss}} with the dissertation ''Teaching probability in the elementary school: an exploratory study'', supervised by John A. Easley Jr. Her dissertation also cites the mentorship of Max Beberman, who died before it could be completed.{{r|diss}} After completing her doctorate, she became an associate professor at [[Wayne State University]] in 1972, and was promoted to full professor in 1978.{{r|retire}} She served as a [[Fulbright Scholar]] in [[Belize]] in 1994,{{r|fulbright}} and again in Romania in 1998.{{r|retire}} At Wayne State, she also directed the master's program in teaching, the Women, Minorities, and Handicapped Program in Education, and a mathematics education institute, and chaired a commission on the status of women at the university.{{r|msmcm}}

Gipson married her second husband, William Lawrence Simpson, in 1980.{{r|obit}} While teaching at Wayne State, she lived across the nearby Canadian border in [[Windsor, Ontario]]. Her husband died in 2005,{{r|obit}} and she retired as a [[professor emerita]] after 35 years of service at Wayne State in 2007.{{r|retire}} She died in Windsor on January 31, 2012.{{r|obit}}

==Books==
Gipson was the coauthor of ''Consumer and Career Mathematics'' (with L. Carey Bolster and H. Douglas Woodburn, Scott & Foresman, 1978){{r|ccm}} and ''[[Black Mathematicians and Their Works]]'' (with [[Virginia Newell]], L. Waldo Rich, and Beauregard Stubblefield, Dorrance & Company, 1980).{{r|bmw}} She also edited ''Impetus, the Black Woman: Proceedings of the Fourth National Congress of Black Women of Canada'' (1978), and self-published ''Changing Faces of Romania'' (2000).

==Recognition==
Mount St. Mary's College named Gipson their outstanding alumna of the year for 1990.{{r|remembering|msmcm}} In 1993, she won the Wayne State University Alumni Faculty Service Award "for her outstanding work on behalf of women, minorities, and the disabled in educational leadership programs".{{r|afsa}} In 2010, the Wayne State University Center for Peace and Conflict Studies gave her their lifetime achievement award.{{r|pcs}}

A scholarship at Wayne State University, the Joella Gipson Endowed Scholarship for Peace and Human Rights Education, is named for her.{{r|esp}}
